scenes.visual: Title card: Gas Exchange and Breathing. Subtitle: Large, thin, moist surfaces.

scenes.tts: Animals take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide by diffusion across large, thin, moist surfaces. Gases move from higher partial pressure to lower. More area, a steeper pressure difference and a thinner barrier all raise the rate. That is why the exchange surface matters. Breathing and blood flow keep the pressure difference up.

scenes.visual: Open on a thin, moist exchange barrier. Show oxygen diffusing from higher to lower partial pressure and carbon dioxide following its own gradient in the opposite direction. Expand the area, steepen the pressure difference, then thin the barrier to show each increasing transfer. Introduce bulk medium flow and blood flow as maintaining the gradients. Use qualitative arrows only.

scenes.tts: This is Fick's law. Partial pressure is one gas's share of the total pressure. Gases dissolve in a water film before crossing cells. So the surface must stay moist.
scenes.narration: This is Fick's law. Partial pressure is one gas's share of the total pressure. Gases dissolve in a water film before crossing cells. So the surface must stay moist.

scenes.visual: Show rate = k × area × partial-pressure difference / thickness. Highlight each factor already introduced. Define partial pressure as one gas's contribution to total pressure. Zoom into the water film and show gas dissolving before crossing cells. Remove the old sea-level arithmetic.

scenes.tts: Breathing renews the gas at that surface. In mammals, the diaphragm flattens and the ribs lift. The chest enlarges, pressure falls, and air flows in. A frog instead raises its mouth floor to push air into the lungs. Mammal air flows in and out through the same airways. This is tidal ventilation.

scenes.visual: Move this scene ahead of the organ comparisons. Animate diaphragm contraction and rib lift enlarging the mammal chest, lowering alveolar pressure below outside pressure and drawing air inward. Contrast with the frog's mouth-floor pump: lower with nostrils open, then close nostrils and raise to push air into lungs. End on reversing arrows in mammal airways labelled tidal ventilation.

scenes.tts: Each breath only partly renews the gas in the alveoli. The windpipe and bronchi are dead space, where no exchange happens. Alveolar ventilation is breathing frequency times the volume of each breath after subtracting dead space. Equal total air movement can mean different amounts of fresh air reaching the alveoli.

scenes.visual: Show fresh gas mixing with gas left in alveoli. Highlight conducting windpipe and bronchi as dead space. Display alveolar ventilation = breathing frequency × (tidal volume − dead space), with parentheses clearly enclosing the subtraction. Compare deeper, slower breaths with shallower, faster breaths at equal minute ventilation, showing less fresh gas reaching alveoli in the shallow pattern. Use qualitative volumes without invented numbers.

scenes.tts: Animals use different surfaces for this shared job. Earthworms exchange gases through moist skin. Insects have branching air tubes called tracheae that reach their tissues. Water holds far less oxygen than air and takes more work to move.

scenes.visual: Introduce comparative exchange surfaces: moist earthworm skin, then insect spiracles and branching tracheae reaching tissues. Compare water and air qualitatively, showing less oxygen per equal volume of water and greater work to move it. Label all panels as examples of diffusion across exchange surfaces.

scenes.tts: A trout's gills have filaments carrying thin plates called lamellae. Inside each lamella, blood runs opposite to the water. This countercurrent exchange keeps a partial-pressure difference along its whole length. Blood leaving can approach the oxygen partial pressure of incoming water.
scenes.narration: A trout's gills have filaments carrying thin plates called lamellae. Inside each lamella, blood runs opposite to the water. scenes.visual: Show gill filaments and thin lamellae as a large-area, thin-barrier solution. Animate water and blood moving in opposite directions, with a maintained oxygen partial-pressure difference along the entire lamella. Outgoing blood approaches incoming water's oxygen partial pressure. Remove the same-direction comparison to keep the scene short; use no numerical bars.

scenes.tts: Bird lungs exchange gas in tubes called parabronchi. Air sacs act as bellows. Through most parabronchi, air flows the same way during breathing in and out. Capillaries cross the airstream. This is crosscurrent exchange.

scenes.caption: Bird lungs exchange gas in tubes called parabronchi. Air sacs act as bellows. Through most parabronchi, air flows the same way during breathing in and out. Capillaries cross the airstream. This is crosscurrent exchange.
scenes.visual: Distinguish the bird's exchange tubes from its ventilating air sacs. Show air sacs acting as bellows and the same airflow direction through most parabronchi during both inspiration and expiration. Show blood capillaries crossing the airstream, labelled crosscurrent exchange. Do not add a two-breath routing claim or a performance ranking.

scenes.tts: What controls breathing? In humans at rest, carbon dioxide sets most of the drive. It enters the brain and lowers the fluid's p H. Central chemoreceptors detect that change. The carotid bodies respond mainly to low arterial oxygen, and also to carbon dioxide. With carbon dioxide production unchanged, less alveolar ventilation lets alveolar carbon dioxide pressure rise.

scenes.visual: Show carbon dioxide entering the brain and lowering extracellular-fluid pH, detected by central chemoreceptors. Show carotid bodies at the carotid artery forks, labelled mainly low arterial oxygen, also carbon dioxide. Connect these sensors to breathing adjustment. At fixed carbon dioxide production, show reduced alveolar ventilation raising alveolar carbon dioxide partial pressure. No molecular receptor details or invented thresholds.

scenes.tts: One-way airflow also occurs in alligators and some lizards. Alligators have no air sacs. So air sacs are not required for one-way flow.

scenes.visual: Close the ranked findings with birds, alligators and some lizards sharing a one-way airflow symbol. Highlight the alligator's lack of air sacs. State: Air sacs are not required for one-way flow. Do not infer an ancestral origin or rank animal performance.
End card: Gas Exchange and Breathing. Recall diffusion, ventilation and chemical control with the same barrier, pump and sensor icons used in the film.
